description: Heilbronn-based team on Field Shift. We're building a web app that helps farmers compare their crop rotation with climate-ready alternatives, using NASA data (POWER, MODIS, SMAP) and validating them against German weather stations. I'm Young, an Information Engineering student at TUM focused on data science and geospatial data. Looking for: frontend/web mapping (JS), agriculture know-how, UX/video storytelling, and German speakers. All levels welcome!
summary:
Crop Circles is a bilingual (English/German) web platform that helps sugar beet farmers in Germany's Kraichgau plan their crop rotations together. The reed planthopper spreads SBR and Stolbur, diseases that reduce sugar content and leave the beet rubbery. Its nymphs overwinter in winter wheat sown after beet and fly to the beet around it, so one farm switching crops alone barely helps.
Using NASA HLS imagery, we tested 3,476 beet parcel-seasons (2023–2025). Beet next to such a "nursery" lost more leaf by late summer (NDRE −0.03, p < 0.001), and the effect fades within a few hundred metres. On that basis the platform finds every nursery in the region and ranks which fields should switch. Switching the right fifth removes 37 % of the pressure; a random fifth removes about 20 %.
For each farmer, it explains four field risks in plain words (planthopper, erosion, drought, heat) using seven NASA datasets (HLS, MODIS, SMAP, GPM IMERG, POWER, NASADEM, ECOSTRESS). It ranks rotations by the farmer's priorities and lets them plan 2026–2030 on their own plots. It also connects neighbours with the plant-protection office, turning satellite data into one shared decision.
details:
Interactive MVP: https://crop-circles.streamlit.app/?lang=en

What it does and how it works

Crop Circles is a bilingual (English/German) web platform for sugar beet farmers, advisors, and the plant protection office in the Kraichgau, Baden-Württemberg. It is built around one problem: the reed planthopper, which spreads SBR and Stolbur in sugar beet. Its nymphs overwinter in winter wheat sown right after beet (a "nursery") and fly to the beet around it in early summer. One farm changing its rotation alone barely helps.

  • My field: four risks in plain words (planthopper, soil washing away, dry summers, heat), each with a level, the field's own numbers, what helps and the source. A satellite view shows which parcels became nurseries this season, a year before official crop maps appear.
  • What to grow: rotations ranked live by the farmer's priorities (soil, water, nitrogen, planthopper, income). A plot planner lets the farmer cut and merge their own plots and paint crops for 2026–2030. Rotation-rule violations appear in red, and each plan is compared with the best match across six criteria. Saved plans are shared anonymously, so neighbors' real crops count in the pressure.
  • Our region: every parcel since 2018, showing which ones spread planthoppers and which receive them. Choosing the right fifth of the nurseries removes 37% of the pressure, compared with about 20% for a random fifth.
  • Neighbors: a regional feed for notes, questions, alerts to the plant-protection office and the office's warnings to the region.

  • How we know: all 18 datasets (7 from NASA), the method, a glossary and every license.

Evidence from NASA data

We read NASA HLS (Sentinel-2) imagery for 3,476 declared beet parcel-seasons (2023–2025). Beet next to a nursery lost more leaf by late summer (NDRE −0.03, p < 0.001, same sign in every season and index). A distance fit puts the planthopper's flight range at about 350 m, a value not reported in the literature. The planner uses it, and the advice becomes concrete: talk to the neighbor whose wheat touches your beet. We report this as an exposure–symptom association, not a measured infection.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Farmers: they see their own risk and options in units they already use (liters per m², days, "7 of the last 10 years").
  • Advisors and sugar companies: they see where coordination pays off most.
  • The plant-protection office: it receives field alerts with the field's figures attached and can warn the region.

The aim is fewer SBR losses through coordinated rotation, which no single farm can achieve alone. The method runs on open data and already works for all of Baden-Württemberg.

Tools and technologies

  • Language and app: Python 3.11; Streamlit app hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, code on GitHub.
  • Data and maths: pandas, NumPy, SciPy and statsmodels for the data and statistics; rasterio, shapely and pyproj for raster and parcel geometry.
  • Charts and maps: Altair charts; deck.gl maps, including a custom HTML/JavaScript map component for the plot planner.
  • Accounts and storage: Supabase (Auth and Postgres) for sign-in, the regional feed and shared plans.
  • Evidence report: matplotlib.
  • Data access: NASA AppEEARS, CMR and LP DAAC cloud imagery, the POWER API and GES DISC; the Copernicus CDS API; DWD open data; and the Baden-Württemberg state's FIONA and LGRB map services.
  • Text and translations: all UI text and content is kept in TOML files, in both languages.
  • Optional AI at runtime: a language model only puts the page's own numbers into words and flags any figure that is not on the page.
  • AI during development: Claude Code and Mistral Vibe, with each use recorded in our AI-use log.
  • Hardware: none beyond laptops.

What makes it creative

  • It treats crop rotation as a neighborhood problem, not a single-field one.
  • It measures the planthopper's flight distance from space instead of guessing it.
  • It turns that number into a planner and a social loop: shared plans, alerts and office warnings.

Factors we considered

  • Farmers first: usable on a phone, plain words, no indices.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: ranges instead of single values, preliminary maps labeled as such, and every nursery checked against a second, independent crop map (DLR).
  • Side effects of switching: erosion and water are weighed alongside the planthopper.
  • Privacy: shared plans carry no names, and secret keys stay on the server.
  • Openness: every number names its source and every dataset its license. The app also works without AI.
